claims.text: The starting material is standard Zircaloy-4 cladding with its native surface condition.
A roughly 1 μm nanostructured chromium coating can be deposited on Zircaloy-4 by magnetron sputtering.
Chromium coatings are a candidate means of improving the high-temperature oxidation resistance of zirconium-alloy cladding.
Optimizing pretreatment, substrate temperature, and interlayer engineering will provide robust coating adhesion and long-term interfacial stability.
During high-temperature steam exposure, the chromium coating will oxidize preferentially to Cr2O3.
The resulting Cr2O3 scale will be adherent and continuous on the coated Zircaloy-4 surface.
A compact Cr2O3 layer acts as a diffusion barrier against further oxidation and oxygen ingress.
The Cr2O3 scale will reduce heat ingress to the underlying Zircaloy-4.
Reduced oxygen ingress through the protective scale will slow oxidation kinetics.
The chromium coating will delay the onset of breakaway oxidation relative to uncoated Zircaloy-4.
At approximately 1200°C in steam for 2 hours, the coating will reduce oxidation weight gain by at least 50% relative to uncoated Zircaloy-4.
The coated cladding will retain the mechanical integrity required for reactor service.
The coated cladding will retain the thermal properties required for reactor service.
The protective effect will hold during severe-accident-like exposure at approximately 1200°C in steam for 2 hours.
The coating will remain suitable under normal reactor operating conditions.
The oxidation benefit depends on the coating maintaining sufficient adhesion and stability during repeated thermal shocks and cycling.
Chromium coatings can peel and crack during high-temperature steam oxidation, creating uncertainty about long-term adhesion.
Extended thermal cycling may cause detrimental interfacial reactions between the chromium coating and Zircaloy-4.
